## Introduction

Child Sexual Abuse (CSA) constitutes one of the most severe adverse experiences in child development with a lifetime prevalence of 11.4% for sexual harassment and 8.7% for any form of hands-on sexual violence [@piolantiGlobalPrevalenceSexual2025]; @worldhealthorganizationRespondingChildrenAdolescents2017\]. The creation, sharing, and viewing of Child Sexual Exploitation Material (CSEM) increased significantly in the last years worldwide [@baskurtMetaanalysisRecidivismRates2024]. Beyond its profound short- and long-term consequences for survivors, CSA represents a substantial challenge for society due to high economical costs [@kewleyPreventingChildSexual2023]. These figures clearly demonstrate the importance of preventing CSA and CSEM.

In CSA and CSEM prevention, a distinction is commonly drawn between primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention programs. Primary prevention initiatives are directed at children and their parents, whereas secondary prevention programs seek to engage adults identified as being at risk for sexual child offenses, but have not yet been convicted. Tertiary programs have the longest history and are designed for individuals who already committed CSA offenses [@kewleyPreventingChildSexual2023]. In recent years, more and more secondary prevention programs have been implemented worldwide [@setoEvaluatingChildSexual2024]. However, @setoEvaluatingChildSexual2024 identified five publications exploring the effectiveness of secondary prevention programs for adults, none of them with a methodological high quality [@kewleyPreventingChildSexual2023]. Thus, currently it is not possible to draw meaningful conclusions on the effectiveness of secondary treatment programs [@setoEvaluatingChildSexual2024]. The effectiveness of tertiary treatment programs for individuals who committed CSA or CSEM has been studied more extensively. In a recent meta-meta analysis (MMA) including 21 meta-analyses on tertiary treatment programs, a treatment effect with an odds ratio (OR) of 0·67, indicating that participants in tertiary treatment programs exhibited approximately a 33% lower risk of recidivism relative to controls was reported [@olverSexualOffenseTreatment2025]. Several moderator variables have been identified: community treatment programs provide higher effect-sizes than institutional treatment programs; individual treatment programs show higher effect-sizes than group programs, high-intensity programs are more effective than low-intensity programs, and the higher the methodological design quality of the study, the lower the effect sizes [@holperModeratorsSexualRecidivism2024; @olverSexualOffenseTreatment2025]. Up to now, most of the mentioned meta-analyses report on tertiary treatment programs for individuals who have been convicted for CSA. The figure for CSEM is not as well studied. A recent review shed light on the methodological weakness of existing studies on the effectiveness of prevention programs for individuals who have used CSEM: mostly, the studies suffer from small sample sizes, too short follow-up periods and a lack of officially registered re-offenses as outcome measure. Besides these limitating factors, the meta-analysis demonstrated preliminary support for the effectiveness of these programs [@gouveiaSystematicReviewEffectiveness2025]. To sum up, meta-there exists a broad empirical basis for a small but significant effectsize in reducing recidivism by tertiary prevention programs. For individuals who have been sentenced for CSEM as well as for secondary prevention programs, the empirical proof of effectiveness is still pending.

Besides this encouraging treatment effects of tertiary intervention programs, there exists a post-release care gap for individuals, who have been sentenced for CSA or CSEM, originating from only having few possibilities of community-based treatment offers since the majority of outpatient therapists working in the primary healthcare system are unwilling to provide treatment for offenders [@schmidtOutpatientTherapistsPerspectives2022; @stiels-glennAvailabilityOutpatientPsychotherapy2010]. Furthermore, most of the above mentioned secondary prevention programs, do not accept already convicted ISAC and ICCSEM under CS for treatment [@beierGermanDunkelfeldProject2015]. Additionally, the number of individuals convicted for the use of child abusive material, raised in the last years resulting in a increased demand for treatment [@baskurtMetaanalysisRecidivismRates2024].

Web-based interventions (WBIs) are assumed to be able to provide a greater accessibility for individuals who face challenges in availing mental health services owing to limited availability resulting in reaching a wider population as it is possible with in-face interventions [@crocamoDigitalHealthInterventions2025]. Meta-analyses demonstrated that stand-alone web-based interventions with professional assistance had greater effect sizes, smaller attrition rates, and larger effect sizes in reduction of psychiatric symptoms [@crocamoDigitalHealthInterventions2025]. It was assumed, that WBIs have also the potential to bridge the gap in the care of individuals with regard to tertiary prevention of individuals with a history of CSA or CSEM offenses [@wildWebBasedHealthServices2019; @hillertWebBasedInitiativesPrevent2024]. To date, there is no empirical evidence available, that WBIs can substantially reduce the risk to re-offense for individuals who already committed CSA or CSEM offenses are scarce [@wildWebBasedHealthServices2019; @hillertWebBasedInitiativesPrevent2024; @schroderWebBasedInterventionsIndividuals2023]. @schroderWebBasedInterventionsIndividuals2023 identified in their review six WBIs implemented in secondary prevention without published data on their effectiveness. Up to now, only one WBI (Prevent It [@latthEffectsInternetdeliveredCognitive2022]) reported on the effectiveness of their WBI. The authors evaluated their guided WBI on a sample of individuals who viewed more than five hours weekly CSEM at baseline, but the minority of their sample reported prior convictions (6.9%) \[@latthChildSexualAbuse2025\]. The participants were recruited mainly via Darknet forums and could take part anonymously. The results showed that, compared with a psychological placebo (n = 78), participants of the intervention arm (n = 76) reported a statistically significant, but small decrease in weekly viewing of CSEM (Cohen’s d 0·18). Besides of some methodological weakness \[@setoEvaluatingChildSexual2024\], this study provides first evidence for the effectiveness of WBIs for secondary prevention of individuals viewing CSEM [@hillertWebBasedInitiativesPrevent2024]. For tertiary prevention programs as well as CSA, to the best of our knowledge, there exists no proof of effectiveness for WBIs.

### Aim of the study

The study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a newly developed WBI in reducing empirically supported dynamic risk factors for re-offending compared to a web-based placebo arm. It aims to evaluate the individual effects of treatment modules within the WBI on reducing dynamic risk factors based on self reports. The primary hypothesis constitutes that participants who take part in the intervention arm show significantly lower values on dynamic risk factors from baseline to inter-, and post-treatment, compared to a placebo arm. We assumed further that, in contrast to the placebo condition, each online module within the intervention arm will reduce the dynamic risk factors targeted in this module in a statistically significant manner. We further assume, that participants in the intervention arm showed lower rates of sexual recidivism in comparison to the placebo arm.
